video_title: The Internet Will Die and So Will You | John West
gist: Wall Street Journal computational journalist John West argues the web is structurally ephemeral (link rot, dead open standards like RSS and Google Reader) and that its modern history is a transfer of agency from users to platforms, consummated the moment an algorithm was inserted between follower and followee. He and Demetri Kofinas trace how the ad-funded, engagement-maximizing model degraded search and sense-making, ask whether AI escapes or repeats that 'enshittification' arc, and close on epistemic collapse — why norms cannot keep pace with the technology, why people cannot tolerate perpetual uncertainty, and why 'neutral algorithm' is an incoherent idea.

themes.theme: Link rot and the web's structural impermanence

insights.claim: John West argues the internet's reputation as permanent and indelible is backwards: ephemerality is built into the web's structure, so digital archives and 'permanent records' decay by default rather than persist.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Any business, index, or dataset built on the assumption that web content persists (citation graphs, training corpora, evidence trails) carries an unpriced decay rate.
insights.quote: It can be that but also it can be a deeply ephemeral place and that ephemerality is baked into the very structure of the web.

insights.claim: West defines a two-stage decay mechanism for the web: sites first suffer content or link drift — a URL redirecting somewhere unexpected, at worst a Bitcoin scam — and then go fully dark to a 404.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Drift precedes death, so redirect-pattern monitoring is a leading indicator of link-graph and archive rot before hard 404s appear.
insights.quote: Linkrod is the phenomenon where a website goes dark where you click on that blue underlined link of text and instead of taking you to a new website it takes you to a 404 page, an error page.

insights.claim: West frames the internet as regenerative rather than static — it persists only through active maintenance and attention, and decays toward entropy without it, a gardening rather than a wilderness model.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Maintenance, not creation, is the scarce input in digital infrastructure; budget archiving and stewardship as recurring opex, not a one-time capex.
insights.quote: just as nature will produce things if left to its own devices, we have a responsibility when we garden to make the soil richer and to shape that natural process into something that is deeply unnatural actually

insights.claim: West's central thesis is that the modern internet's defining story is a transfer of agency from humans to platforms — an outside force with incentives that run against human thriving.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Frames platform regulation and product design fights as agency-allocation questions, the axis on which future antitrust and design-standard pressure will land.
insights.quote: the story of the internet in its modern incarnation is a shift from human agency to platform agency

insights.claim: West claims platforms hold a mechanistic model of human behavior that then reshapes users' own sense of what is possible online, and that users bringing their full selves to social media would damage those companies' bottom lines.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Implies a structural conflict between richer, more deliberate usage and monetization — 'time well spent' style products face an inherent revenue ceiling on ad-funded platforms.
insights.quote: these platforms which are deeply mechanistic in how they think about our behavior and how they think about us and that that infects our own thinking about what is possible and what is desirable online

insights.claim: West and Kofinas locate online 'homelessness' in the fact that users do not own the communities they belong to — displacement, not deletion, is the core harm of walled gardens.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Portability and data-ownership features are the direct answer to the churn risk platforms create; watch protocol-based social products positioning there.
insights.quote: the displacement online that we feel is about a loss of agency. I think it comes back to that loss of agency.

insights.claim: West uses the Google Reader shutdown as the canonical case of platform-caused displacement — killing one client destroyed the shared street layout of the blogosphere and scattered its residents.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Deprecation of a dominant client, not of the underlying standard, is what kills an ecosystem — a risk to price in any single-vendor-dependent open protocol.
insights.quote: when Google Reader went away, they ripped up 12th Street and all of a sudden, you know, the people who lived there had to find new digs

themes.theme: Open standards vs. closed feeds and switching costs

insights.claim: West credits RSS — an open feed standard — with enabling the blogging boom, and blames its replacement by closed feeds such as Facebook's News Feed and X for collapsing the web's interoperability.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Open-standard distribution (RSS still powers podcasts) is the last unmediated channel to an audience; its persistence is why podcasting resisted platform capture.

insights.claim: West singles out X as more hostile to external links than Twitter was, i.e. platforms now actively suppress outbound traffic rather than merely failing to promote it.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Publishers and media businesses dependent on social referral face a structural, not cyclical, decline in traffic — direct and RSS-style channels are the hedge.
insights.quote: or even Twitter now X which is even more hostile to external links

insights.claim: West identifies the precise inflection in social media as the moment an algorithm was inserted between follower and followee — not the arrival of social networking itself — and says that is when the center of gravity shifted.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Dates the regime change for anyone modeling attention markets: pre-algorithmic reach was a function of the follower graph, after it of ranking, which the platform can tax at will.
insights.quote: a shift that I would want to draw a lot of attention to is the moment when it went from being about, you know, I follow you and I see your posts to I follow you and an algorithm sits between you and me and decides which posts I see

insights.claim: West, who says he is normally predisposed to think poorly of markets, argues competition would improve the web and that an open, portable follower graph could unlock a generative new era — but switching costs make Facebook's and LinkedIn's inertia nearly unbeatable.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Mandated graph portability is the single intervention that would reopen social networking to new entrants — the policy lever to watch for incumbent valuation risk.
insights.quote: that switching cost you just described is like makes it really really hard to overcome the inertia of Facebook or LinkedIn or whatever it is

themes.theme: Ad model, two masters, and the enshittification of AI

insights.claim: West argues recommendation systems are structurally conflicted — servants of two masters, satisfying users' real desires while driving revenue for the company that built them — and that the two objectives are frequently in tension.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: A clean test for any feed or assistant product: whose objective function is it optimizing? Subscription-funded rankers are the only ones where the conflict is absent.
insights.quote: they are the servants of two masters all too often. They are the servants of the users who have real desires, but they are really driving revenue for whatever company has built them.

insights.claim: Kofinas frames the last 20-30 years of the web as a shift from serving users to serving advertisers, with users as inventory to be harvested; West agrees.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Keeps the advertising business model, not the technology, as the causal variable behind product degradation — the same test to apply to AI monetization.
insights.quote: we're there as sheep to be sheared, as cows to be milked for these giant corporations

insights.claim: West says AI has not yet undergone the 'enshittification' that platform technologies did, but that its monetization model is simply not yet built — implying today's high AI product quality is a pre-monetization artifact, not a durable property.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: The bull case on AI assistant quality should be discounted for the monetization phase that has not yet arrived; watch for the first ad or commerce injection as the regime marker.
insights.quote: I think that we have not yet seen the to use Cory Dtoro's word which I think is a useful word initification of AI in quite the same way that we have of the platform technologies

insights.claim: West names the specific degradation mechanism to watch for: an AI company tweaking the model so a chatbot's recommendations hawk whatever product it is being paid to advertise.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Native, unlabeled commercial bias inside model outputs would be far harder to detect than sponsored search links — a live regulatory and trust risk for assistant products.
insights.quote: what if we just tweak the model to you know hawk whatever the product is that we're advertising for in line with the recommendations that they give in a chatbot

insights.claim: West expects AI to become very expensive once users pay the full token cost of what they consume, implying current usage is subsidized.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Ad-supported AI is the likely resolution of the subsidy gap — the same path that pushed the web from user-serving to advertiser-serving.
insights.quote: what's going to happen when we actually have to pay the full token costs of what we're doing. I mean I I think it's going to be very expensive.

themes.theme: Vibe coding and the small-web revival

insights.claim: West says AI's most exciting effect is a revival of experimental, personal web-making: he vibe-coded Mixtab, a tiny private social site that turns friends' bookmarks into a shared newspaper edition, in about a week despite lacking the time to build it manually.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Collapsing build cost for micro-social software creates demand for cheap hosting, personal-app tooling, and small-audience products that never cleared the old economics.

insights.claim: West argues the current 'why not just make it' mood among AI-assisted builders feels like the early web, framing AI as a re-decentralizing force at the creation layer even while platforms remain concentrated at the distribution layer.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Cheap creation plus captured distribution is the central tension of the next web cycle — the bottleneck value shifts to whoever controls discovery.
insights.quote: there's this kind of like well why not just make it feeling that a lot of people are having right now that really to me feels a lot like the early web did

insights.claim: West predicts AI will never live up to either its detractors' or its proponents' promises and will instead land somewhere weirder — a middle-path stance against both the doom and the AGI-imminent camps.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Argues against positioning around either the collapse or the singularity scenario; the tradeable path is specific capability adoption, not the extremes.
insights.quote: I think AI is never going to live up to the promises of its detractors or its proponents.

insights.claim: West dismisses 'will AI achieve superintelligence' as a category error and possibly the wrong question, arguing the useful and actionable question is which specific capabilities these systems will have — noting AI is a bundle of very different technologies packaged under one label.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: A capability-level rather than intelligence-level analysis is the one that maps to revenue lines and displacement risk; superintelligence debates carry no actionable information.
insights.quote: I think that it is not a very useful question if AI will achieve super intelligence. I think it is a very useful question to wonder like what are the specific capabilities of artificial intelligence systems going to look like?

themes.theme: Search decay and human-sourced trust signals

insights.claim: West says Google search was already dying before AI: results have degraded into sponsored material at the top, with the best results now found by scrolling to the bottom — an inversion of how Google used to work.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Search-quality erosion predates AI competition, so Google's share loss is partly self-inflicted rather than purely a chatbot substitution story.
insights.quote: I used to go on Google and get great search results. So now I just get a bunch of sponsored crap and I always try to remember to scroll to the bottom of the page where the best results are rather than the top

insights.claim: West reads the mass habit of appending 'Reddit' to Google queries as evidence that users trust human social signal over a heavily gamified ranking algorithm, and that the internet remains fundamentally a social place.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Human-verified content pools become the scarce, licensable asset in an AI-saturated web — the structural basis for Reddit-style data value.
insights.quote: people have been appending Reddit to their search queries in an effort to get the Reddit results for things because that's more trusted often times than the results that are just natively given back from Google

insights.claim: West warns that as more of the internet is written by AI and LLMs are trained on the internet, the feedback loop threatens both the corpus and the humans entangled with it — a self-consuming knowledge supply.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Pre-AI human text becomes a dated, non-renewable asset; owners of verified human corpora hold pricing power over model builders.

insights.claim: West holds that meaning is made by humans and is not an independent fact of the world, while information may be external — making meaning-making the essential human function AI cannot simply assume.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Defines where human labor stays defensible as generation costs fall: judgment and meaning attribution rather than information retrieval.
insights.quote: I think meaning is something we bring to the world. It is not an independent fact of the world outside of it.

themes.theme: Epistemic collapse, norms lag, and algorithmic values

insights.claim: West's explanation for why past technology panics were overblown is that societies had time to build social norms around use — and he argues the internet, social media and AI now move far faster than norms can form, making this cycle genuinely different from television, the novel, or writing.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: The norms-lag framework predicts regulatory and backlash risk scales with adoption speed — the reason AI's compressed timeline raises policy risk above prior technology waves.
insights.quote: the internet and AI and social media all moves so much faster than our norms are capable of keeping up with

insights.claim: West says he is glad the modern distribution system for conspiracy theories did not exist during 9/11, and predicts that in today's ecosystem such theories would spread farther, faster and stranger.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Implies the next mass-casualty or crisis event produces far more severe narrative fragmentation, a tail risk for policy response and market-relevant crisis coordination.
insights.quote: I think we would see that spread farther and faster and stranger than before.

insights.claim: Kofinas argues institutional gaslighting plus shattered priors — the 2008 financial crisis and COVID revealing long-held beliefs to be false — makes populations reprogrammable into equally absurd new realities, because people cannot live in perpetual uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Demetri Kofinas (host)
insights.so_what: Credibility shocks at institutions are followed by belief-migration, not agnosticism — a repeatable pattern for anticipating post-crisis political and narrative regime shifts.
insights.quote: people in the end cannot live in a perpetual state of uncertainty. They need to believe in something that's concrete even if it's not true.

insights.claim: West argues knowledge production is an underappreciated, thorny human process — at the Wall Street Journal it is extremely hard to say only true things and not even imply false ones — which is why claims that AI will 'solve journalism' by being unbiased miss what the work actually is.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: AI-replaces-journalism theses underrate the embodied judgment layer; the defensible media asset is verified process, not article volume.
insights.quote: you have to be an embodied person with other embodied people at some level and you have to be in the muck trying your best to produce real knowledge from that

insights.claim: West offers a process-over-outcome trust protocol: trust not that a speaker is right but that they are running a process that is more often right than not — which Kofinas notes lets you assess credibility without domain expertise.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: A portable due-diligence heuristic for evaluating analysts, research providers and AI outputs when you lack subject-matter knowledge.
insights.quote: I try to trust not that the people who are saying the thing are say are right but I try to trust that the people are when they are doing a process that is more often right than not.

insights.claim: West identifies 'vice signaling' as the current online status mechanic — an inversion of virtue signaling where people gain credibility by saying increasingly distressing things they may not even believe, and end up believing them later.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Explains why platform discourse ratchets toward extremity independent of politics — brand-safety risk for advertisers rises structurally, not cyclically.
insights.quote: you have this kind of weird inverse of it where people actually gain credibility by saying increasingly distressing things that even they might not think are okay

insights.claim: West's Leaves of Grass experiment — embedding Walt Whitman stanza by stanza and serving more of whatever he dwelled on — unexpectedly kept him engaged, demonstrating that engagement optimization is nearly content-neutral yet has severe content consequences.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Engagement mechanics work on any corpus, so blaming content rather than ranking design misdiagnoses the problem — and the same mechanics will transfer directly into AI interfaces.
insights.quote: the longer I spent I dwelled on each stanza, the more stanzas I would get like that. And I thought it was just a dumb exercise that was not going to work. And it actually kept me engaged.

insights.claim: West rejects the idea of a neutral algorithm outright: any constructed ranking system necessarily carries bias — toward engagement, friends, or something else — and will amplify some voices over others by construction.
insights.speaker: John West
insights.so_what: Undermines 'neutral platform' defenses in both regulation and litigation; the enforceable question becomes which values a ranker encodes, not whether it is biased.
insights.quote: it is not the case that there is a neutral algorithm that would equally amplify voices on the left and the right
